name: Career Overview
markdown:
Physical therapists (PTs) evaluate how people move and help them improve physical function, manage pain, and participate in activities that matter to them. Their patients include people recovering from injury or surgery and people living with longer-term conditions. Physical therapy also addresses preventing movement problems and maintaining function.

The work combines examination, clinical reasoning, treatment, and teaching. A PT chooses a plan for an individual patient rather than handing everyone the same exercise sheet. The current U.S. professional entry degree is the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT), followed by the licensing process; this is a different profession from a physical therapist assistant or personal trainer.

name: Duties and Responsibilities
markdown:
The therapist connects findings from an examination with a treatment plan:

- **Evaluate movement:** Review the person’s history and examine movement, strength, balance, function, and other relevant factors.
- **Set goals and plan care:** Identify practical goals with the patient and choose interventions appropriate to the findings.
- **Provide treatment and instruction:** Use therapeutic movement, hands-on care, education, and other appropriate approaches; teach safe use of prescribed movement or equipment.
- **Reassess:** Compare the response with earlier findings, revise the plan, and recognize when another professional’s evaluation is needed.
- **Coordinate and document:** Record progress, communicate with the team, and direct appropriate work by assistants and support personnel.

The examination and ongoing decisions distinguish a therapist’s role from simply supervising a workout.

name: A Day in the Life
markdown:
In an illustrative outpatient day, a PT alternates between evaluations and follow-up appointments. A new patient explains what has become difficult, and the therapist examines relevant movement before discussing goals. A returning patient reports how the previous plan worked outside the clinic; the PT observes performance and decides whether to change it.

The therapist also documents findings, communicates with colleagues, and makes sure the patient understands the next steps. A session is not successful merely because an exercise was completed: the response helps guide the next decision.

In a hospital, the immediate goal might be safer mobility before discharge. In home care, the therapist can see the actual space where the person needs to move. Those settings change the day’s priorities.

name: Work Environment and Schedule
markdown:
PTs work in outpatient offices and clinics, hospitals, nursing facilities, and patients’ homes. Most work full time; some appointments occur in the evening or on weekends. Much of the job involves being on one’s feet and actively working with patients.

A clinic may have specialized exercise equipment and a repeated appointment schedule. A home visit requires adapting to the person’s surroundings and available space. Hospital care involves close coordination with other clinicians and the patient’s current medical needs. The environment affects both the treatment options and how much contact the therapist has with a person’s caregivers.

name: Skills, Knowledge, and Personal Qualities
markdown:
Physical therapy requires knowledge of anatomy, physiology, movement, and how illness or injury affects function. The therapist must connect measurements and observations with the patient’s account of daily life. A stronger movement test matters most when the improvement helps the person do something useful.

Teaching is equally important. Patients need explanations they can understand, opportunities to ask questions, and feedback while practicing. Clinical reasoning includes noticing when a planned activity is not appropriate and changing course. Accurate records make it possible to compare progress rather than relying on memory or an impression that the patient “looks better.”

name: Physical and Emotional Demands
markdown:
The job can involve standing, bending, demonstrating movement, and helping people move safely. Equipment, team assistance, and appropriate handling methods protect patients and clinicians. NIOSH emphasizes that moving people manually can cause injury and that safe-handling systems are more reliable than expecting a worker to manage every transfer alone.

Patients may feel pain, worry about recovery, or become discouraged when change is slow. A PT needs patience without promising a particular result. Maintaining attention across several appointments while completing documentation can also be demanding. Different settings place different physical and scheduling demands on the therapist.

name: Education and Training
markdown:
The current professional entry route in the United States is a CAPTE-accredited Doctor of Physical Therapy program. APTA describes professional DPT programs as typically three years; most require a bachelor’s degree first. Some offer combined undergraduate/professional pathways, so the total time after high school depends on the program.

Coursework includes science, movement, clinical reasoning, communication, and supervised clinical education. A student should distinguish a professional DPT program from a general exercise science degree and from a physical therapist assistant program. Those programs prepare for different roles.

High-school biology, chemistry, physics, mathematics, and communication build useful foundations. When comparing DPT routes, check prerequisites and the clinical education sequence as well as the degree title; early preparation helps students understand both the academic work and the patient-care commitment.

name: Certification and Licensure
markdown:
Physical therapists must meet state licensing requirements. The National Physical Therapy Examination (NPTE), administered through the Federation of State Boards of Physical Therapy, is an important step toward licensure; it is not the license itself.

In Kansas, the State Board of Healing Arts evaluates PT applicants. K.S.A. 65-2906 requires qualifying education, the required examination, an application, and applicable fees, among its qualifications. The Board’s rules and application process determine the documentation needed.

The DPT is an academic degree. State licensure authorizes practice. Later board certification in a specialty recognizes additional expertise. Keeping these separate helps students understand why earning a degree or a specialty credential does not replace the licensing process.

name: Salary, Entry-Level Earnings, and Job Outlook
markdown:
BLS reports a **May 2025 U.S. median annual wage of $102,760** for physical therapists. Half of workers earned more and half less; this does not describe a new graduate’s starting salary or Kansas-specific pay.

BLS projects **12% employment growth from 2025 to 2035**, with about **13,400 openings per year** on average. Openings include replacements for people leaving the occupation as well as new positions.

These figures describe physical therapists, not physical therapist assistants. When comparing education and career options, keep the cost and duration of the DPT route separate from the shorter preparation for other rehabilitation roles.

name: Specialties and Career Advancement
markdown:
Physical therapists can develop expertise in areas such as orthopedics, neurology, pediatrics, geriatrics, sports, and cardiovascular or pulmonary care. The American Board of Physical Therapy Specialties recognizes advanced clinical expertise through specialty certification. Working with a particular patient group and becoming a board-certified specialist are related but distinct.

Other career directions include teaching, clinical leadership, research, and managing a practice. A specialist may continue substantial direct patient care. Choosing a direction depends on whether a therapist most enjoys clinical complexity, developing colleagues, investigating evidence, or organizing services.

name: Benefits and Challenges of the Career
markdown:
One appeal is connecting scientific reasoning to a patient’s everyday goals. Progress can be visible: moving with more confidence or returning to an activity that matters. The work offers repeated opportunities to explain, observe, and refine a plan rather than relying on a single encounter.

Challenges include physical demands, documentation, busy schedules, and helping patients whose progress is slower or more limited than hoped. Professional education is a substantial commitment. A rewarding practice needs realistic expectations and attention to the patient’s own goals, not a promise that everyone will recover in the same way.

name: Career Connections and Related Occupations
markdown:
**Physical therapist assistants** carry out selected treatment components under a PT’s direction; becoming a PT requires the therapist education and licensing route. **Occupational therapists** emphasize participation in everyday activities, including adapting tasks and environments. **Athletic trainers** provide prevention, injury care, emergency response, and rehabilitation within their professional framework.

These roles can overlap in rehabilitation teams. For example, a PT and OT may both work with someone after a stroke, while emphasizing different aspects of movement and daily activity. Their collaboration is more useful to understand than a rigid claim that only one profession addresses a particular body part.

name: Could This Career Interest You?
markdown:
Are you interested in how movement works and why a person has difficulty with it? Would you enjoy observing carefully, explaining a plan, and adjusting it based on the response? Could you support someone through repeated practice without promising rapid improvement?

Compare a hospital PT role with outpatient or home-based work. Ask how therapists choose goals, recognize meaningful progress, and divide time between direct care and records. An observation opportunity, when available through an approved program, can show how much reasoning happens around the visible exercises.

name: Professional Associations
markdown:
The [American Physical Therapy Association (APTA)](https://www.apta.org/apta-and-you/about-us) supports physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, and the profession through education, professional resources, and advocacy. Its [ChoosePT](https://www.choosept.com/) resource explains physical therapy to the public.

APTA’s career and specialty information can help students explore practice settings and later development. A professional association is different from the Kansas licensing board and from the organization administering the NPTE.
